overview: Picture a confederation moving between cold mountain pastures and busy Silk Roads towns. The Karluks were never one frozen tribe or a tidy modern country. In the early 700s, their leaders served and fought larger Türk empires; then Karluks joined the revolt that broke the Second Türk empire, lost a struggle with the Uyghurs and moved west. They helped the Abbasid side win at Talas in 751 and by 766 controlled Suyab and Talas under a ruler called yabghu. Herds, irrigated fields, workshops, caravans and several religions met in their realm. After 840, some rulers claimed higher prestige, but the later Qarakhanid dynasty cannot safely be called simply “the Karluks.” Islam spread gradually, especially after Samanid forces captured Talas in 893, while named Karluk groups continued for centuries. The atlas adds two giant caution signs: its 700 polygon lies far east of the later heartland, and the target vanishes at 800 and 1000 despite being indexed continuously. Treat its shapes as snapshots from an imported historical dataset, not hoofprint-perfect borders.

periods.title: A federation between larger empires
periods.summary: Karluk groups north of the Tien Shan moved between Western and Eastern Türk power, rebelled in 711 to 714 and were named as enemies in the 732 Kül Tigin memorial.

periods.title: Coalition victory, Uyghur defeat and a westward turn
periods.summary: Karluks helped overthrow the Second Türk rulers, then lost the struggle with the Uyghurs and moved toward the Tien Shan as older alliances broke apart.

periods.title: Talas and entry into Semirechye
periods.summary: Karluk forces aided the Abbasid side at Talas; by 766 Karluk leaders controlled Suyab and Talas after years of conflict among Tang, Tibetans and Türgesh factions.

periods.title: The Karluk yabghu’s pasture-and-city realm
periods.summary: A Karluk-led confederation held much of Semirechye, combining mobile pastoral zones with Sogdian-founded towns, irrigated fields and long-distance commercial routes across generations.

periods.title: New prestige after the Uyghur collapse
periods.summary: After the Uyghur empire fell, Karluk rulers are reported claiming higher steppe titles, but the path from their yabghu polity to Qarakhanid rule remains disputed.

periods.title: Samanid pressure and gradual Islamization
periods.summary: Ismail ibn Ahmad captured Talas in 893; Muslim communities and mosques expanded eastward while religion still varied among mobile groups and multicultural towns.

periods.title: Qarakhanid ascendancy and Karluk continuity
periods.summary: Qarakhanid rulers converted and expanded, taking Bukhara permanently in 999. Karluk tribes continued, but equating the whole later dynasty with one Karluk state is unsafe.

sections.title: Begin with the atlas, including its missing centuries

items.text: The exact target is karluks, labelled “Karluks” and indexed circa 700 to 1000. Initial coverage called it an approximate state with two mapped intervals, 700 to 800 and 900 to 1000, and no card. Those ranges describe atlas files, not three centuries of one fixed border or government.

At 700 the target is one Polygon with one ring and 16 coordinate positions, a small eastern outline rather than a continent-wide claim. Its bounds are [84.55944559445595, 39.71380489249975, 101.05121051210511, 46.205906017734634], and its coordinate SHA-256 is f9cf29d6bbd20652b1d201baa40210f20ff4e830c86a984173b3f79ad3d93f6d. Those figures come from decoded coordinates.

That 700 shape contains Beshbalik/Jimsar but misses Suyab, Balasagun, Taraz, Talas, Issyk-Kul and Ili. A separate Western Turk feature covers several western points, while Göktürk and Tibetan features cover other tested places. The map shows an eastern snapshot, not the later Karluk heartland.

The target disappears entirely at 800, although this is the best-documented century of the Karluk yabghu around Suyab and Talas. At 900 it returns as a much larger, west-shifted 138-position Polygon, bounds [64.94644946449466, 39.68339044940879, 91.33471334713346, 46.682859784388384], hash 1020a34a849e86cad0216d704c81a64a35f26250a877e53415a3fda167c592bd. The change is geometrically dramatic.

The 900 shape includes Suyab, Balasagun, Taraz, Talas, Issyk-Kul, Ili, Beshbalik, Tashkent and Otrar, but misses Kashgar, Fergana, Samarkand and Bukhara. Karluks vanish again at 1000; the separately indexed karkhanids appear only at 1100. These are atlas seams, not proof of mass disappearance.

sections.title: A mobile federation emerged between rival Türk powers

items.text: Early Karluks were a federation rather than a single bloodline or nation-state. One eighth-century inscription presents three component groups, while a later geographical work counts seven. The different numbers probably reflect changing coalitions and labels, so neither should be frozen into an eternal tribal checklist.

Chinese accounts place Karluk groups around the upper Irtysh and northern Tien Shan under Western Türk authority in the mid-seventh century. Their economy was strongly pastoral. Subordination did not erase their own leaders, followers or ability to change alliances when imperial power weakened.

Eastern Türk rulers extended control over them in the early eighth century, but Karluks rebelled during 711 to 714. That conflict belongs before the atlas polygon’s later westward story: it helps explain why a group seen east of the Tien Shan could become a major actor farther west.

Karluks joined Basmils and Uyghurs against the Second Türk empire in 742 to 745. Victory did not create a Karluk empire: Uyghur leaders won the contest among the allies, defeated Karluk forces and pushed many west. Confederation politics could turn yesterday’s teammate into tomorrow’s pursuer.

The atlas has separate gokturk, western-gokturk-khaganate and uyghurs ids; no independent Türgesh id was found in the audited index. Those data choices must stay distinct from history: Karluks served, fought and succeeded parts of these coalitions without becoming aliases for every Türk-speaking neighbor.

sections.title: War and diplomacy carried them toward Suyab and Talas

items.text: Tang forces captured Suyab in 748, and an Abbasid army with Karluk support defeated the Tang near Talas in 751. The sources agree Karluks mattered in the battle; accounts differ over timing and motives, so the familiar tale of one perfectly timed battlefield betrayal deserves caution.

Talas did not make Karluks the inventors of paper. Papermaking already existed in China and paper reached western markets before 751; the story of captive artisans founding the first Samarkand mill may be partly legend. A dramatic battle is memorable, but technology travels through longer networks.

By 766 Karluk leaders had taken Suyab and Talas and eliminated competing Türgesh khagans after prolonged factional war. Their ruler used yabghu, a prestigious title below khagan. This was a new regional balance built from migration, alliance and seizure, not an empty land awaiting arrival.

Suyab itself had been founded and developed largely by Sogdians before Karluk rule. Its roads, craft quarters and shrines connected Chinese, Sogdian, Turkic and other communities. Capturing a city meant governing inherited people and infrastructure, not replacing everyone behind its walls overnight.

Muslim geographers later placed the Karluk to Oghuz frontier near Isfijab on the middle Syr Darya and Karluk settlement south of Issyk-Kul. Some Karluk groups reached upper Oxus country. These reports describe a broad, shifting human landscape; they do not outline a surveyed sovereign border.

sections.title: A yabghu governed people, routes and negotiated loyalties

items.text: The early paramount leader was called elteber under Türk overlords; later the western confederation’s ruler was a yabghu. Neither title automatically meant an all-powerful khagan. Authority depended on component groups, military followers, pastures, towns and deals with neighboring courts, and could weaken when alliances shifted.

A Karluk yabghu joined Sogdian and Tibetan interests in supporting the rebel Rafi ibn Layth against Caliph Harun al-Rashid. That episode shows Karluk diplomacy working across language and religion. It also warns against drawing clean civilizational teams on a frontier full of temporary partnerships.

The Uyghur empire’s collapse in 840 changed steppe prestige, and later traditions associate Karluk rulers with claims to the title khagan. Evidence for the exact moment and succession is thin. A higher title could announce ambition without proving a centralized replacement empire appeared on schedule.

Qarakhanid origins remain debated because early internal narratives are lost and coins do much of the historical work. Karluk, Chigil, Yaghma and Uyghur explanations have all been proposed. The safest wording is that Karluks were an important component, not that every Qarakhanid was simply a renamed Karluk.

Satuk Bughra Khan’s conversion near Kashgar, his death around 955, the reported mass conversion around 960 and the conquests of Bukhara in 992 and 999 belong to Qarakhanid history. They explain transformation near the atlas endpoint without turning the whole 700 to 1000 card into one dynasty.

sections.title: Herds, fields, workshops and caravans shared the landscape

items.text: Pastoral families managed sheep, horses, cattle, camels and goats, while towns and foothill oases supported grain and garden agriculture. Mobile people needed manufactured goods and settled food; towns needed animals, transport and wool. The Karluk economy worked through those connections, not a herder-versus-farmer wall.

Irrigation sustained much Central Asian cultivation, especially around older Sogdian settlements. Karluk rule inherited canals, fields and skilled communities rather than inventing them. Exact eighth-century yields around Suyab are unknown, so the card does not turn regional agricultural patterns into a fake harvest spreadsheet.

Sogdian merchants had dominated many overland routes under earlier Türk protection. Their networks weakened after Tang withdrawal, partly revived under Uyghurs and changed again under Samanids. Karluk territory sat within this moving system of caravans, tolls, diplomacy and multilingual brokerage.

Silk, musk, silverwork, amber, medicinal plants, perfumes, precious metals and enslaved people appear among long-distance goods. A caravan catalogue reveals regional exchange and exploitation; it does not mean each Karluk household owned exotic perfume or that every traveller crossed the whole route.

Coins show changing public languages. Earlier Western Türk issues in Semirechye carry Sogdian inscriptions; ninth- and tenth-century “proto-Qarakhanid” issues increasingly use Arabic Kufic. Numismatists do not label every coin Karluk, but the sequence reveals institutions that outlived a single ruling coalition.

sections.title: Belief changed by town, camp and century

items.text: The 732 Kül Tigin inscription invokes the sky god Tengri and a sacred Türk political world, useful context for early Karluk rivals and allies. It is an external elite monument, not a Karluk creed. The reviewed sources do not preserve one statement of belief spoken for every Karluk group.

Suyab’s archaeology includes Buddhist sanctuaries, a Zoroastrian cemetery and Nestorian Christian churches. Their dates and users vary, but together they show that Karluk rulers inherited a religiously mixed city. A shrine inside their realm did not automatically convert every herding family outside it.

Contact with Muslim merchants, towns and courts began before mass conversion. The Samanid ruler Ismail ibn Ahmad attacked and captured Talas in 893, and tenth-century geographers noted mosques in towns east of Talas. Islamization was a process with uneven local timing, not one day’s switch.

Ak-Beshim also produced crosses, Christian objects, Turkic-Sogdian inscriptions and a later manuscript codex. Several finds come from tenth- or early eleventh-century contexts. They illuminate the city’s long transition, while their presence cannot identify the religion or literacy of an unnamed Karluk household.

UNESCO describes Ak-Beshim and Burana as Silk Roads towns where Indian, Chinese, Sogdian and Turkic traditions met. That broad heritage framing is useful, but its tentative-list boundaries and later monuments should not be mistaken for the exact Karluk polygon or a single-period settlement plan.

sections.title: Families and children are visible mostly around the edges

items.text: A confederation joined named groups under leaders and followers, so kinship and political loyalty mattered, but the sources reviewed do not give an ordinary Karluk family size, marriage age or household rulebook. Royal titles tell us about rank more readily than affection, adoption or daily care.

Society included mobile pastoral households, warriors and chiefs, along with farmers, merchants, artisans and religious specialists in towns. These categories overlapped and were unequal. Sources spotlight male rulers, while women’s herding, textile, food and family work is plausible but seldom individually documented for Karluks.

No surviving Karluk school register or child’s exercise survives from 700 to 1000 in the reviewed evidence. A Chinese account says Sogdian boys in Kang began book and commercial study at five; that is useful urban comparison, not permission to assign the same classroom to every Karluk child.

Pastoral children probably learned animal care, routes, tools and weather through household work, an inference from the economy rather than a Karluk lesson plan. Children in multilingual towns could encounter Sogdian, Turkic, Chinese and later Arabic writing, but access depended on family, occupation and status.

Archaeologists at Ak-Beshim combine excavation, ground-penetrating radar, animal-bone study, plant remains and radiocarbon dating. That teamwork can reconstruct activities rulers ignored. Even so, identifying a small object as a child’s possession is difficult because adults also spun thread, played games and lost things.

sections.title: Homes, clothes, food, work and play changed across the centuries

items.text: Mobile pastoralists used portable shelters and felt-working traditions, while towns had mud-brick buildings. No excavated structure can be securely labelled a standard eighth-century “Karluk tent.” The honest picture allows tents, camps and city houses without pretending one floor plan served everyone.

Late tenth-century Ak-Beshim houses had two-room plans, wall benches, ovens and domestic pottery; tools included knives, awls, beads and spindle whorls. These are valuable atlas-end, early Qarakhanid-transition clues. They cannot be copied backward unchanged into a Karluk camp of 720.

Felt, rugs, leather footwear, horse equipment and jewelry belonged to regional pastoral manufacture and exchange. Directly dated Karluk wardrobes are scarce, so bright costume reconstructions should be labelled artistic. Clothes had to handle riding and weather, but no source supplies one mandatory Karluk outfit.

Late tenth- to early eleventh-century Ak-Beshim deposits contain sheep and goat most often, then cattle and some horse, plus barley, wheat, millet, lentil, grapes, melons, apples, pear and pomegranate. This is an urban transition menu and waste record, not three centuries of identical Karluk dinners.

A worn, perforated sheep ankle bone was catalogued as a chuko game piece, and excavators noted a possible ceramic bell. Both come from the late occupation horizon; player age and the bell’s use remain uncertain. Archaeology gives us a game clue, not a complete tournament bracket or concert programme.

sections.title: Medicine, water and toilets require unusually careful labels

items.text: A modern study of Tibetan medical histories finds a notice connecting the physician Harina with Garlok, interpreted as Qarluq. This is a later textual tradition, not a surviving Karluk medical manual or excavated clinic. It hints at knowledge exchange but cannot reconstruct everyday diagnosis, herbs or surgery.

Medicinal plants travelled in Central Asian trade, but a commodity list is not a prescription. Families surely cared for injury, childbirth and illness, yet the reviewed sources do not securely identify a Karluk healer’s kit or treatment recipe. The card therefore keeps practical medicine largely unknown.

Water supported animals, irrigated fields and dense towns. At Ak-Beshim, one late pit may have been a well or toilet, but excavators found no clear water-flow trace and later refuse filled it. Ambiguity is the result: one hole cannot confidently be both plumbing diagram and privy.

Another deep pit was cautiously called a presumed toilet because of its contents and stratigraphy. Both sanitation candidates date around the late tenth or early eleventh century, near or just beyond the atlas endpoint. Neither proves that eighth-century Karluk camps or towns used the same arrangement.

Excavated streets had gravel and slag surfaces, but the studied section produced no confirmed ditch for rainwater or sewage. Burana preserves later bathhouse and water-main evidence from Qarakhanid urban life. No secure 700 to 900 Karluk latrine, sewer or hygiene rule survives in the reviewed record.

sections.title: One stone sentence names the Karluks, but from outside

items.text: The Kül Tigin memorial was erected in 732 for an elite of the Second Türk empire. Its Turkic sides use the right-to-left Old Turkic runiform script, while another face carries Chinese. It is contemporary evidence about Karluks from a rival court, not a Karluk-authored national monument.

Original script, Kül Tigin North 1: “𐰚𐰇𐰠𐱅𐰃𐰏𐰤 : 𐰘𐰃𐱅𐰃𐰆𐱃𐰔 : 𐰖𐱁𐰃𐰭𐰀 : 𐰴𐰺𐰞𐰸 : 𐰉𐰆𐰑𐰣 : 𐰼𐰇𐰼 : 𐰉𐰺𐰆𐰺 : 𐰼𐰚𐰠𐰃 : 𐰖𐰍𐰃 : 𐰉𐰆𐰡𐰃”. It is a complete carved sentence on the memorial monument, and the visible qarluq bodun words mean “Karluk people” in its own political context.

Transliteration: “Kül Tigin yiti otuz yašïna qarluq bodun ärür barur ärklï yaγï boltï.” Translation: “When Prince Kül was twenty-seven years old, the Karluk people became an enemy who began to act freely and independently.” Punctuation and spelling follow a modern scholarly edition.

The sentence reports conflict from the victors’ memorial voice. It proves that the name Qarluq/Karluk was politically meaningful in 732 and records an independence claim. It does not prove every Karluk spoke exactly the monument’s prestige dialect or could read its script.

After the Karluk yabghu polity transformed, named Karluk groups remained under Qarakhanid and later rulers. Towns, herding networks and families also continued while titles and faiths changed. Continuity of people and practices is real; it should not be rewritten as one uninterrupted state lasting forever.

ending.text: There was no single day when all Karluks vanished. A conventional political transition around the mid-tenth century marks the rise of Qarakhanid rulers, but their tribal origins remain disputed and their Islamization unfolded over time. Qarakhanids captured Bukhara permanently in 999, while Karluk-named groups, pastoral work, towns and trade continued under new governments. The atlas carries karluks to 1000 but has no exact feature in that snapshot, then draws a separate misspelled karkhanids id at 1100. This bundle therefore treats about 940 as a cautious transformation marker, not a conquest that erased a people.
